solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Light blue marks on bird fluttering in its home?

indicators.note: a bird's fluttering suggests its letters flapping about out of order
the marks and the jumbled bird sit inside the word for the bird's home

blocks.note: a caged bird's home
M is the abbreviation for the German mark
the word bird with its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A bird flapping about its cage leaves pale blue marks on itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light blue' looks like a description of the marks, but it is the definition; the bird's home is its cage.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambridge blue is the pale shade worn by Cambridge University sportsmen, so the university name stands for that colour.

clue.text: Chaplain behind jaw in the kirk

blocks.note: CH is a standard abbreviation for chaplain
aft means at or towards the back

explanation.surface: A minister's jaw seen from behind during a church service in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The kirk is the Scottish church, so 'in the kirk' marks a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaft is the Scots dialect word for the jaw or jawbone, often used in the plural.

clue.text: Player of medley goes from this, like contact between pilots aloft

definitions.text: Player of medley goes from this

blocks.clueFragment: Player of medley goes from this
blocks.note: a medley is a string of tunes, so its player moves from one tune to the next
describing communication or combat between two aircraft in flight

explanation.surface: A musician running through a medley, set beside radio chatter between airborne pilots.
explanation.walkthrough: An air is a tune, so the medley player goes from air to air; the same phrase is the aviation term.
explanation.definitionFit: Air-to-air describes anything passing between aircraft in flight, and a tune is also called an air.

clue.text: Lives twice interrupted by love

indicators.note: something interrupted has another thing put into its middle

blocks.note: bis is Latin for twice, used in music and numbering
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone whose life has twice been disrupted by romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Bios is a short form of biographies, written accounts of people's lives; it is also Greek for life.

clue.text: Where dogs are set on rodents dodging trap, just the thing

definitions.text: Where dogs are set on rodents

indicators.note: dodging means darting about, so the letters move out of their places

blocks.note: the word trap with its letters rearranged
'it' as in 'that's it', exactly what is wanted

explanation.surface: Rats escaping a trap meet terriers, which suits the dog owner perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rodents dodging trap' reads as a scene, but rodents belongs to the definition and only trap is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat-pit was an enclosure where terriers were set to kill rats, once a popular betting sport.

clue.text: Seine (say), wrong, free, rising up once wholly decayed

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising up means reading the string from bottom to top

blocks.note: a seine is a kind of fishing net, hence the (say)
a tort is a civil wrong in law
to rid is to free of something

explanation.surface: A grim picture of the river Seine rotting, with something wrong to be freed.
explanation.walkthrough: Seine looks like the Paris river, but it is a fishing net. 'Once' marks the answer as an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirt-rotten is an archaic compound meaning completely rotten, decayed right through.

clue.text: Some with allergies avoid this surfeit, half of mutton

blocks.note: a glut is an excess supply
mutton is printers' slang for an em space, and half an em is an en

explanation.surface: Allergy sufferers avoiding a surfeit of mutton at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of mutton is not MUT or TON: printers call the em space a mutton, and half of an em is an en.
explanation.definitionFit: Gluten is the protein in wheat that coeliacs and people with wheat intolerance must keep out of their diet.

clue.text: Shred songs Spooner-style? He may well be deaf

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: to shred is to rip apart
Lieder are German art songs, said like 'leader'
the two words said with their opening sounds exchanged

explanation.surface: Ripping up song sheets, Spooner-fashion, with a nod to a deaf listener.
explanation.walkthrough: Say RIP LIEDER with the opening R and L exchanged and you hear the answer; Lieder is pronounced 'leader'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lip-reader understands speech by watching mouth movements, a skill many deaf people rely on.

clue.text: Dance? No thanks, it’s obscure for poet

indicators.note: 'no thanks' asks for the word for thanks to be removed

blocks.note: the veleta is an old round dance in triple time
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: Turning down a dance invitation, then a remark that something is unclear to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Spenser used vele for veil; 'for poet' marks the poetic form.
explanation.definitionFit: To veil something is to obscure or hide it, and vele is the old poetic spelling of veil.

clue.text: Sort of foot-lever let out to disentangle inside

indicators.note: let out suggests letting the letters loose to fall into a new order
the word for disentangle is placed within the other letters

blocks.note: the word let rearranged
redd is a Scots word for tidy or disentangle

explanation.surface: Instructions for freeing a jammed foot pedal by letting it out.
explanation.definitionFit: A treddle is a variant spelling of treadle, the pedal that drives a loom or sewing machine.

clue.text: Former duke dismissing flanking pages showing scars

indicators.note: dismissing the flanking items means dropping what stands at either end

blocks.note: Prince Philip, the late Duke of Edinburgh
p is the abbreviation for page, so two pages are P and P

explanation.surface: A former duke sacking his attendant pages and revealing old wounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip with a P removed from each end leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hili is the plural of hilum, the scar on a seed left where it was attached to its stalk.

clue.text: Hairs of a kind in the ears, not so sensible

indicators.note: something in the ears is heard rather than seen written

blocks.note: cilia are tiny hairlike projections on cells

explanation.surface: A remark about hairs growing in the ears being rather foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic accent, cilia and the answer are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Sillier is the comparative of silly, meaning more foolish, the opposite of more sensible.

clue.text: In tumult old militiaman gets detached from Tim

indicators.note: detached from means the named letters break off and are lost

blocks.note: a timariot held land in the Ottoman Empire in return for military service
the name taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly soldier losing touch with a friend called Tim amid chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: Tim looks like a stray character, but it is the front of TIMARIOT, removed to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A-riot is an adverb meaning in a state of riot, disorder or uproar.

clue.text: Prince in position of steersman round a riverside French commune

indicators.note: the steersman's position goes round the following letter, enclosing it

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for prince
a helmsman steers with his hand on the tiller
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prince taking the helm of a boat by a commune on a French river.
explanation.walkthrough: A sits inside ON TILLER, after its T, and P goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Pontailler-sur-Saône is a small commune in Burgundy on the banks of the river Saône.

clue.text: Glasgow bum after a drink begged endlessly (penniless)

indicators.note: endlessly says the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: rum is a spirit
pled is a past tense of plead, beg

explanation.surface: A down-and-out in Glasgow, broke, cadging money for drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The lost D is old shorthand for a penny, which is why '(penniless)' sits there.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumple is Scots for the rump or buttocks, and Glasgow marks it as a Scottish word.

clue.text: Water bird I caught on lake, served in pastry

indicators.note: a filling served in a pie is enclosed by its crust

blocks.note: a pie is a pastry dish
taken as written
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a tarn is a small mountain lake

explanation.surface: A cook boasting of catching a water bird on a lake and baking it in a pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' simply sets the caught letter before the lake; the whole string is baked inside the pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: Pictarnie is a Scottish dialect name for a tern, a slender seabird.

clue.text: Dot and Peter naughtily messed about

indicators.note: behaving naughtily means not keeping to proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two children, Dot and Peter, misbehaving and making a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: To potter is to busy oneself in an aimless, unhurried way, which is messing about.

clue.text: Struggle in net

blocks.note: first meaning: hard, exhausting work
second meaning: a snare or net for game

explanation.walkthrough: 'Struggle in net' paints a trapped animal; the two words are separate senses of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both laborious effort and, usually in the plural, a snare for catching prey.

clue.text: Murrayfield ground? That’s armful I scattered

indicators.note: 'that's X' says the answer is what remains once the given letters are taken from the whole
scattered things are strewn about in no fixed order

blocks.note: Murrayfield is the rugby stadium in Edinburgh
taken as written, the letters to be removed

explanation.surface: A rugby stadium's turf, carried off by the armful and strewn around.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite: the answer plus ARMFUL I, jumbled, spells Murrayfield; removing those letters leaves R, Y, E, D to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Yerd is Scots for earth or soil, and Murrayfield sets the Scottish context for that ground.

clue.text: Type of paste to chill in gruel, stirred (8, two words)

indicators.note: stirring a pot mixes its contents into a new arrangement

blocks.note: to ice is to chill
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe step: chill the paste by mixing it into stirred porridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Rice glue is an adhesive paste made by boiling rice flour in water, used in Japan and China.

clue.text: Quiet sort of green lining recess

indicators.note: a lining sits inside something, so these letters go within the next word

blocks.note: pea green is a shade of green
an apse is a vaulted recess in a church

explanation.surface: A calm green paint colour inside an alcove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' looks like an adjective, or P for piano; it is the verb definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease is to pacify or calm someone, which is to quiet them.

clue.text: Peter’s friend powdered in talc containing fragrant oil

indicators.note: powdered means ground down, so the letters are broken up and remixed
containing says the jumbled letters hold the next item inside

blocks.note: the letters of in and talc rearranged
otto, or attar, is a perfume oil from rose petals

explanation.surface: Someone's friend Peter dusted with talc and perfumed oil.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter is Peter Rabbit in Beatrix Potter's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Cottontail is one of Peter Rabbit's sisters, alongside Flopsy and Mopsy, in Beatrix Potter's tales.

clue.text: Tripped lightly, free of stones, round savoury snack

indicators.note: round means going about the next item, enclosing it

blocks.note: fruit that is pitted has had its stones removed
a tapa is a Spanish savoury snack

explanation.surface: Someone tripping daintily round pitted olives and bar snacks.
explanation.walkthrough: Tapas are small Spanish bar snacks; one of them is a tapa.
explanation.definitionFit: To pitapat is to move with quick light steps, so pitapatted means tripped along lightly.

clue.text: No longer trim I kept in lying flat

indicators.note: something kept in is held inside another word

blocks.note: taken as written
prone means lying face down

explanation.surface: Someone out of shape kept in bed, lying flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' marks the answer as an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Proine is an old form of prune, meaning to trim or preen.

clue.text: Examination applied to a bit of old silver

blocks.note: a test is an examination
on as in placed against or applied to

explanation.surface: An assay run on a piece of antique silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit' is a coin, not a small piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A teston was an old silver coin, struck in Europe and Tudor England.

clue.text: Hat sailor wears back to front – he’s a fool

indicators.note: back to front means the order runs from the end to the start

blocks.note: a tarpaulin, or tarp, is a sailor's waterproof hat

explanation.surface: A sailor wearing his hat the wrong way round looks foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: Tarpaulin is both a sailor and his hat, so 'hat sailor wears' is one clue to TARP.
explanation.definitionFit: Prat is British slang for an idiot or foolish person.

clue.text: Sandy’s underground den, requiring very little money

blocks.note: wee means tiny
m is a short form of money, as in million

explanation.surface: A cheap underground hideout owned by a man called Sandy.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy is a crossword stock Scotsman, marking a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Weem is a Scots word for a cave or earth-house, an underground dwelling.

clue.text: Unit of landed herrings one wrapped in special string

indicators.note: something wrapped in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a means one
in ancient Greek music the mese is the middle string or note

explanation.surface: A catch of herrings brought ashore, each one tied with string.
explanation.definitionFit: A mease is a measure of herrings, traditionally five hundred fish.

clue.text: A role he’s mangled for listeners

indicators.note: something mangled is crushed out of its proper shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An actor botching his part in front of the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listeners' suggests an audience, but it is the body parts that listen.
explanation.definitionFit: Earholes are the ears, the organs a person listens with.

clue.text: Leading officer flourished lost banner with joyful cry

indicators.note: lost says those letters go missing from the word that follows

blocks.note: a flag is a banner
fl. abbreviates floruit, Latin for flourished
ha is an exclamation of triumph

explanation.surface: A commanding officer waving a banner and cheering, then losing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flourished' looks like waving the banner, but it is fl., the floruit abbreviation, taken out of FLAG.
explanation.definitionFit: An agha is a commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire, a title of rank.

clue.text: Old couple, people ageing ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very end of the word, its final letter

blocks.note: men means people
the final letter of ageing

explanation.surface: An elderly pair, people slowly growing old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old couple' reads as an aged pair, but couple is a verb and old marks an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Meng is an obsolete verb meaning to mix or join together, which is to couple.

clue.text: Digital problem maybe affected Anglia broadcast

indicators.note: something affected is altered from its natural state
broadcast seed is thrown about and lands in no order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A technical fault disrupting an Anglia Television broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital problem' suggests a signal fault; digital here means of the fingers. Anglia TV is a regional British broadcaster.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnail is a hangnail, a torn strip of skin beside a fingernail, so a trouble of the digits.

clue.text: Musk’s asset? ‘Equates with lavender’ – there you’ll have it

indicators.note: the letters are there in the quoted words, waiting to be picked out across their join

blocks.note: the closing letters of the word
the opening letters of the word

explanation.surface: A slogan likening a tech billionaire's prize asset to a fragrant herb.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the join of 'Equates' and 'lavender', with 'with' putting them side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Tesla is the electric car company that Elon Musk heads, one of his chief holdings.

clue.text: Boozer opening to give away? Hurried along

indicators.note: opening means prising apart, so the next word is split to take the first one inside

blocks.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub
to shed is to cast off or give up

explanation.surface: A pub opening its doors to offer free drinks, and people rushing there.
explanation.walkthrough: Boozer looks like a drinker; it is the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: To shin is to run or move quickly on foot, so shinned means hurried.

clue.text: Talent negative, not useful

blocks.note: no is a negative reply
US is short for unserviceable, meaning useless

explanation.surface: A harsh verdict: no talent, nothing useful.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is practical intelligence or common sense, a natural aptitude akin to talent.

clue.text: European in Kolkata? He accompanies clique in service as of old

indicators.note: to accompany is to go alongside, so the two items sit side by side
in places the preceding letters inside the word for service

blocks.note: a ring is a closed group or clique
taken as written
in feudal times a fee was land held in return for service

explanation.surface: A colonial-era man joining an exclusive set in old-fashioned service in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As of old' flags the feudal sense of fee, land held in return for service. The question mark admits Kolkata is one example of where the word was used.
explanation.definitionFit: Feringhee was the Indian name for a European, especially a Portuguese or Briton, in colonial times.
